title: Iran retaliates with charges of its own
subtitle: Alleges killing of Iranian in B.C. was a 'criminal' act
article: The Chretien government held its fire Thursday after Iran launched a counterattack in the diplomatic row over the killing and burial of a Montreal photojournalist, accusing police in British Columbia of the "criminal" killing of an Iranian.
"Based on what we know, we don't think the situations can compare," Foreign Affairs spokesman Reynald Doiron said.

Iran's accusations stemmed from a July 14 incident in Port Moody, B.C., during which Iranian Keyvan Tabesh,18, was shot and killed by a plainclothes officer after Tabesh lunged at him with a machete in an apparent road-rage incident.

Tehran insisted on a rapid, transparent inquiry, with wording that mirrored the Canadian government's demands for an investigation into the torture and killing by Iranian officials of Zahra Kazemi, 54, and the prosecution of those responsible.

An Iranian government press release announced Thursday that there is "fear and horror" among Iranians in Canada following the shooting of Keyvan. "Why have the Canadian police, who should safeguard the security of the people, committed this disgraceful crime which scared Iranian citizens living in Canada," Iranian state media quoted Foreign Ministry spokesman Hamid Reza Asefi as saying, adding that the shooting was a "criminal" act.
That came as news to the Tabesh family in Burnaby, B.C.
"We were surprised," said Keyvan's sister, Rita, in an interview at her home. "We never talk to the government."

Rita said as soon as she learned that news of her brother's death was being mentioned by Iranian government officials, she phoned her husband, who is visiting relatives in Iran, to ask him to phone TV stations there and tell them to stop broadcasting the news. Rita and Keyvan's father, Nasser, said Keyvan's death was not the business of the Iranian government.

Pari Saeedi, a spokeswoman with the Iranian-Canadian Community of Western Canada, said the Iranian government's comments are in direct retaliation for the Canadian government's demand for answers in Zahra Kazemi's death. "This is bullying and the Canadian government should not buy it," said Saeedi, who left Iran in 1985. "They're covering their crime."

Tehran's attempt to draw a parallel between the two cases began less than 24 hours after Prime Minister Jean Chretien announced he was pulling Canada's ambassador to Iran back to Ottawa to protest Kazemi's killing and her burial Wednesday.

Canada is mulling penalties against Iran, including economic sanctions and curbs on government-to-government contacts and travel, and is exploring legal and religious options for having the body exhumed and brought to Canada.

"There is no moral equivalence at all to police officers in Canada fulfilling their duties, and always being subject to full investigation ... and a regime like Iran's which consistently tortures and murders its own citizens and now the citizens of other countries," said Canadian Alliance foreign affairs critic Stockwell Day.
Foreign Affairs Minister Bill Graham was not available for comment, but officials said he wants to talk with his Iranian counterpart Kamal Kharazi.
